Causal functions form a separated presheaf that is a sheaf exactly when the space admits no "solipsistic contextuality", so tight spaces give a sheaf and some dynamical causal structures do not, letting deterministic local data fail to glue. Adds an enabling relation to a measurement scenario and reads contextuality as a game: the Experimenter chooses measurements, Nature chooses outcomes, and Nature's deterministic strategies replace the event sheaf. Flat scenarios and Gogioso and Pinzani's Bell scenarios with a causal order come out as special cases, and Experimenter strategies express adaptive measurement, as in the Anders–Browne GHZ OR-gate. Its sharpest point is that the strategy presheaf is not a sheaf: deterministic, compatible local strategies can fail to glue (Example 7.2) or glue non-uniquely (Example 7.3). Two colloidal particles in optical traps are coupled by the fluid through a symmetric tensor, and the trap of one is moved by recorded Ornstein–Uhlenbeck noise. Mutual information, time-delayed mutual information and transfer entropy, estimated from experimental and simulated trajectories, recover drive → driven particle → other particle. They show backflow between the particles at the measured drive strengths, and one-way flow at strong drive in simulation only. Stronger coupling lowers the information the driven particle shares with the drive and raises what the particles share, in parallel with a reported trend of irreversibility under coarse-graining. Without drive the particles are statistically independent. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-788](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-788.md)) in full; worth reading as a clean experimental benchmark for directional information measures: two colloids, symmetrically coupled by the fluid, one trap moved by recorded noise, with transfer entropy and time-delayed mutual information recovering drive → driven → other particle. Read it knowing that the drive acts on one particle and is recorded, so the measures locate where a drive enters; they do not tell a shared drive from coupling, and the direction they report changes with drive strength while the coupling stays symmetric. Held for [QUESTION-063](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-063.md) as a limit on what such measures can see, in [THEORY-275](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-275.md). |
| [LIT-961](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-961.md) v2 | A Reply to Makelov et al. (2023)'s "Interpretability Illusion" Arguments | Wu, Geiger, Huang, Arora, Icard, Potts and Goodman (2024). The authors of distributed alignment search reply to Makelov et al. (2023). They argue that the "illusion" is generic, because a direction a model uses need not be orthogonal to the null space of the next layer; that FLDD can be large with no change in behaviour; and that the factual-recall cases come from DAS trained per fact pair. Their toy counterexample holds only for an unnormalized patch. Both papers grant that alignments related by a change of basis can tie under interchange interventions. The reply's own GPT-2 experiments agree that MLP8 carries almost no name-position information (4% IIA, against 70% for the layer-8 block output). | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-809](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-809.md)) in full; worth reading for the point it shares with the paper it answers: interchange interventions on one set of variables can be satisfied equally by alignments related by a change of basis, so the mediating variable is fixed only relative to a choice of units. Read it knowing that its central toy computation, which claims Makelov et al.'s test rejects their own faithful direction, holds only for an unnormalized patch; patching the subspace the rowspace component spans recovers the full effect. Its own GPT-2 experiments agree that MLP8 carries almost no name-position information. The dispute is over the label, the metric (FLDD against IIA) and how DAS is trained, not over constitution against correlation. Filed, with [LIT-968](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-968.md), as [THEORY-243](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-243.md). |
| [LIT-968](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-968.md) v2 | Is This the Subspace You Are Looking for? An Interpretability Illusion for Subspace Activation Patching | Makelov, Lange and Nanda (2023). A subspace activation patch can make a model behave as if a feature had changed while the patched direction is the sum of a part that varies with the feature but cannot reach the output (in an MLP, the kernel of the down-projection) and a part that can reach the output but is dormant on the data. Exact in a three-unit network; shown for MLP8 of GPT-2 Small on indirect object identification and for GPT2-XL MLPs on factual recall, where the effect vanishes once the disconnected part is removed. A residual-stream direction for the same feature passes the test. One-dimensional fact patches and rank-1 edits are nearly interchangeable, so a working rank-1 edit does not show the fact is stored in the edited layer. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-782](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-782.md)) in full; worth reading as the clearest case of an intervention that produces the predicted counterfactual output without the intervened variable carrying the feature: a subspace patch that pairs a direction varying with the feature but unable to reach the output with one that can reach it but is dormant on the data. Read it knowing that its ground truth for GPT-2's MLP8 comes from prior component-level work, that it concedes a cancelling-subspaces reading it does not test, that its own residual-stream case passes the test, and that the reply ([LIT-961](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-961.md)) contests the label but not the MLP8 measurements. It speaks of faithfulness to a computation, not of constitution. Filed as [THEORY-282](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-282.md) and, with the reply, [THEORY-243](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-243.md). |
| [LIT-987](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-987.md) v2 | Internal Causal Mechanisms Robustly Predict Language Model Out-of-Distribution Behaviors | Huang, Tao, Icard, Yang and Potts (2025; ICML 2025). Given a high-level causal model of a task and the subspace where DAS locates its key variable on correct in-distribution examples, transplanting a test input's value of that variable into verified examples (counterfactual simulation) predicts whether the output is correct. In Llama-3-8B-Instruct, over five tasks and ten shifts that keep the task but lower accuracy, it beats output confidence and causal-agnostic probes on 8 of 10. A probe of the located variable beats a probe of its orthogonal complement on 7 of 10. Interchange accuracy and predictive power rise together only until accuracy nears 1. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-765](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-765.md)) in full; worth reading as a measured case in which variables located by interchange intervention as mediating a model's in-distribution behaviour predict whether its outputs stay correct under task-preserving shifts better than output confidence or probes of the rest of the representation. Read it knowing that it is one model, two selected shifts per task and three folds without significance tests; that counterfactual simulation wins 8 of 10 shifts and the causal-variable probe beats the background probe on only 7; that its comparison features are not "merely correlated" ones; and that it claims nothing about constitution. It does not cite Makelov et al. or the reply. Filed as [THEORY-287](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-287.md). |
| [LIT-1038](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1038.md) | Quantifying causal emergence shows that macro can beat micro | Hoel, Albantakis and Tononi (2013), PNAS 110(49). Effective information, the mutual information between uniformly imposed interventions and their effects, equals effectiveness (determinism minus degeneracy) times the log of the state-space size. Coarse-graining always loses size and can gain effectiveness, so in four toy systems of logic gates a macro description carries 0.40 to 2.92 bits more than the micro it supervenes on. The claim that the EI peak is where causation happens rests on the uniform intervention distribution imposed at each level. | Active — read in full 2026-10-13 ([NOTE-726](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-726.md)) from the PubMed Central PDF of the published article (PMC3856819, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3856819/pdf/pnas.201314922.pdf), fetched through the Internet Archive capture of 2022-11-13 because PMC answered scripted requests with a reCAPTCHA page and pnas.org returned 403; the online Supporting Information was not read. Worth reading as the source of effective information as a measure of causal emergence: it shows exactly when a coarse-grained description of a known mechanism can carry more EI than the micro, and its macro advantage rests on imposing a uniform intervention distribution at each level. For [QUESTION-093](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-093.md) it is an interventional criterion met with no closure and no self-individuation; it complements [CLAIM-154](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-154.md) and [THEORY-133](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-133.md) and is neither a case nor a rival of them; it measures a different object from the information-decomposition account of [LIT-025](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-025.md). |

| [LIT-1164](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1164.md) | Causal Reasoning in Graphical Time Series Models | Eichler & Didelez (2007), UAI 2007: 109–116, [ARXIV-1206.5246](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.5246). Defines the causal effect of an intervention on one component of a stationary multivariate time series on another at a later time, and links it to strong Granger noncausality through mixed graphs (directed edges for Granger causality, dashed edges for contemporaneous dependence). Under its intervention assumptions, which require the system to include every relevant process and exclude instantaneous causality, a missing directed edge means no effect at the next step, non-ancestry means none at any horizon, and back-door and front-door criteria identify the effect from observational data. In a Gaussian VAR the identified effect is a coefficient of the multi-step linear predictor. | Active — read in full 2026-10-16 (NOTE-941); worth reading as the short statement of exactly when a Granger-causal analysis says something about interventions: under its intervention assumptions, which need the series to include every relevant process (observed or not) and exclude instantaneous causation, a missing Granger edge means no causal effect at the next step and non-ancestry means none at any horizon, and time-series back-door and front-door criteria identify effects from observational data. Read it knowing that the front-door theorem's proof is deferred to a paper "in preparation", that the results are sufficient conditions, and that the examples are Gaussian VARs. Filed as THEORY-704. |
| [LIT-1165](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1165.md) | Information Flows? A Critique of Transfer Entropies | James, Barnett & Crutchfield (2016), *Physical Review Letters* 116, 238701, [ARXIV-1512.06479](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.06479). Defines information flow from X to Y as information in Y attributable solely to X's past, and shows with two XOR processes that transfer entropy is not it. With Y_t = X_{t−1} ⊕ Y_{t−1}, T_{X→Y} = 1 bit, yet the bit is jointly carried by both pasts (co-information −1). With Z_t = X_{t−1} ⊕ Y_{t−1}, both transfer entropies are 0 and the causation entropies are 1 bit each. By PID, transfer entropy is unique plus synergistic information; only the unique part is a candidate for flow. Conditioning is not subtraction. | Active — read in full 2026-10-17 (NOTE-945); worth reading as the short, exact case that transfer entropy is not a measure of information flow: in two XOR processes it credits a bit to a source that holds none of it alone, and reports zero for sources that jointly fix the target. Read it knowing that "flow" is defined by the authors as information solely attributable to one source's past, that the cure it points to (unique information) has no agreed measure, and that its conjecture that directed information and Ay and Polani's interventional flow fail the same way is a conjecture. Filed as THEORY-707. |
| [LIT-1166](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1166.md) | Causality, Feedback and Directed Information | Massey (1990), Proc. ISITA-90, Waikiki. The usual definition of a discrete memoryless channel, P(y^N\|x^N) = Π P(y_n\|x_n), holds only when the channel is used without feedback; the right definition is P(y_n\|x^n y^{n−1}) = P(y_n\|x_n). Defines directed information I(X^N→Y^N) = Σ_n I(X^n; Y_n \| Y^{n−1}), after Marko (1973), and proves I(X^N→Y^N) ≤ I(X^N;Y^N) with equality without feedback, that it bounds what the output tells about the source in a causal system, and so that feedback does not increase DMC capacity. "Statistical dependence, unlike causality, has no inherent directivity." | Active — read in full 2026-10-17 ([NOTE-939](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-939.md)); worth reading as the short source of directed information, I(X^N→Y^N) = Σ I(X^n; Y_n \| Y^{n−1}), and of the point that the usual definition of a memoryless channel silently forbids feedback because it confuses statistical with causal dependence. Read it knowing that "causal" here is a factorization condition on a system of sources and channels, not an interventional notion; that directed information conditions on the current input as well as the past, so it is not transfer entropy; and that the copy read is the author's preprint, not the proceedings version. Filed as [THEORY-711](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-711.md). |
| [LIT-1169](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1169.md) | Measurement of Linear Dependence and Feedback between Multiple Time Series | Geweke (1982), *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 77(378): 304–313. Measures the linear dependence between two multivariate time series as the sum of three parts: feedback from the first to the second, feedback from the second to the first, and instantaneous feedback. The directed measures are log ratios of generalized variances (determinants of residual covariance matrices), have asymptotic χ² null distributions, and decompose additively by frequency. Unread; known through Barnett, Barrett and Seth and the abstract. | Unavailable — unread, registered 2026-10-16. A lawful copy was sought and not reached: OpenAlex marks it closed with no repository full text, Crossref lists only the Taylor & Francis and JSTOR copies, and web searches found no author-posted or course-hosted copy. Its generalized-variance measure and χ² asymptotics are restated by Barnett, Barrett and Seth ([LIT-1171](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1171.md)), which is how the record reads it until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-1170](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1170.md) | Measuring Autonomy and Emergence via Granger Causality | Seth (2010), *Artificial Life* 16(2): 179–196. Defines G-autonomy, the log ratio of a variable's prediction-error variance without and with its own past, given external variables, and G-emergence, a macro variable's G-autonomy from micro variables times their mean Granger causality on it, so that it is zero if the macro variable is independent of the micro or fully predicted by them. In a predator–prey model an evolved controller has higher G-autonomy than a reactive rule; in a boids model, flocking has higher G-emergence and more macro-to-micro Granger causality than random or rigid motion. Measures are linear or Taylor-expanded nonlinear regressions. | Active — read in full 2026-10-16 ([NOTE-935](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-935.md)); worth reading as the source of G-emergence, the Granger-based measure the causal-emergence readings name as a rival ([NOTE-726](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-726.md), [NOTE-791](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-791.md), [NOTE-010](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-010.md)). Read it knowing that its measures are predictive and relative to a regression model and a variable set, as Seth himself says (§5.2), so that "downward causation" here means Granger causation from a macro variable to micro variables, and that the validation is two agent-based models with hand-chosen conditions. Filed as [THEORY-703](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-703.md). |
| [LIT-1171](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1171.md) | Granger causality and transfer entropy are equivalent for Gaussian variables | Barnett, Barrett & Seth (2009), *Physical Review Letters* 103, 238701, [ARXIV-0910.4514](https://arxiv.org/abs/0910.4514). For jointly Gaussian stationary processes X, Y, Z, Geweke's Granger causality F_{Y→X\|Z} = ln(\|Σ(X\|X⁻⊕Z⁻)\|/\|Σ(X\|X⁻⊕Y⁻⊕Z⁻)\|) equals 2T_{Y→X\|Z}, twice the transfer entropy, for multivariate predictor, predictee and conditioning variables. The proof is two lines: Gaussian conditional entropy is ½ln\|partial covariance\| plus a constant, and OLS residual covariance is the partial covariance. | Active — read in full 2026-10-16 (NOTE-934); worth reading as the short, exact source of the Gaussian equivalence the record already leans on through Barnett and Bossomaier (NOTE-053): for jointly Gaussian stationary processes, Geweke's generalized-variance Granger causality is exactly twice the transfer entropy, conditional and multivariate. Read it knowing that the identity is about population quantities at fixed lags, that sample agreement depends on how the entropies are estimated, and that the remark that a stationary Gaussian AR process leaves nothing for nonlinear Granger causality cites unpublished work. Filed as THEORY-700. |
| [LIT-1173](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1173.md) | Investigating Causal Relations by Econometric Models and Cross-spectral Methods | Granger (1969), *Econometrica* 37(3): 424–438. Proposes testable definitions of causality and feedback between stationary time series: Y causes X if the past of Y improves the prediction of X beyond what the other relevant past information gives. Shows the cross spectrum can be decomposed into two parts, one for each causal arm of a feedback loop. Unread; known through the works that restate it. | Unavailable — unread, registered 2026-10-16. A lawful copy was sought and not reached: Crossref and the Econometric Society give only the JSTOR copy (stable 1912791), behind a login; a course-hosted copy on a University of Freiburg seminar page (jeti.uni-freiburg.de, stud_sem_SS_09/grangercausality.pdf) refused this client's connection three times and answered WebFetch with HTTP 503; a Bilkent course copy found by search returned 404. Searched again on 2026-10-17: the Freiburg host still reset the connection, and the only other copies found (ResearchGate, Scribd) are user uploads whose authorization could not be established. The record reads it through Barnett, Barrett and Seth ([LIT-1171](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1171.md)), Seth ([LIT-1170](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1170.md)) and Eichler and Didelez ([LIT-1164](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1164.md)), which restate its definition, until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-1174](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1174.md) | Information Flows in Causal Networks | Ay & Polani (2008), *Advances in Complex Systems* 11(1): 17–41. In a causal Bayesian network, X_B is causally independent of X_A imposing X_S if setting x_A after setting x_S does not change the post-interventional distribution of X_B; this holds for every model on a DAG iff every directed path from A to B meets S (ud-separation, Theorem 2). Information flow I(X_A → X_B \| X̂_S) is conditional mutual information with every probability replaced by its interventional counterpart, and is zero iff causal independence holds (under positivity of p(x_S)). Examples show it differs from mutual information and from transfer entropy: two binary chains that swap states have zero transfer entropy and one bit of flow (at k = 1, by the record's check), and an observationally identical pair of independent inverters has zero of both. | Active — read in full 2026-10-17 ([NOTE-946](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-946.md)), from the authors' preprint dated 12 May 2006; worth reading as the interventional counterpart of transfer entropy: information flow I(X_A → X_B \| X̂_S) is conditional mutual information computed from do()-distributions instead of observational ones, it vanishes exactly under a graphical condition (ud-separation), and examples show it differs from transfer entropy and conditional mutual information in both directions. Read it knowing that it needs the full causal Bayesian network and its mechanisms, not data; that the examples are deterministic binary networks; and that its Example 6 claim of one bit holds, by the record's calculation, only for k = 1 or when imposing X_k alone. The published version (Advances in Complex Systems 11(1), 2008) was not compared. Filed as [THEORY-710](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-710.md). |
| [LIT-1177](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1177.md) | Measuring Information Transfer | Schreiber (2000), *Physical Review Letters* 85, 461, [ARXIV-nlin/0001042](https://arxiv.org/abs/nlin/0001042). Defines the transfer entropy T_{J→I} = Σ p(i_{n+1}, i_n^{(k)}, j_n^{(l)}) log[p(i_{n+1} \| i_n^{(k)}, j_n^{(l)}) / p(i_{n+1} \| i_n^{(k)})], the Kullback entropy of assuming that I's transitions do not depend on J's past, with history lengths k and l ("most natural" l = k or l = 1). Unlike time-delayed mutual information it is directional and zero for static correlation. In a tent-map lattice it is O(ε²) in the coupling while time-delayed MI is zero, and in an Ulam-map lattice it shows the coupling's direction where time-delayed MI does not. | Active — read in full 2026-10-17 (NOTE-940); worth reading as the four-page source of transfer entropy, which the record uses in seven documents without holding it: T_{J→I} is the Kullback entropy of the transition probabilities of I with and without the past of J, at history lengths k and l that the definition leaves open. Read it knowing that "information transfer" and "exchange" are the paper's words for a conditional mutual information, that common inputs are excluded only when they are known and conditioned on, that the continuum-limit claim is asserted, and that the evidence is two coupled-map lattices and one physiological pair, the last of which Schreiber himself says a common trigger could explain. Filed as THEORY-701. |
| [LIT-1244](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1244.md) v2 | Reconciling emergences: An information-theoretic approach to identify causal emergence in multivariate data | Rosas et al. (2020). Defines causal emergence of a supervenient feature V as unique information about the system's future that no group of k parts holds, Un⁽ᵏ⁾(V_t; X_t′ \| X_t) > 0, and proves a system has such a feature iff Syn⁽ᵏ⁾(X_t; X_t′) > 0, with the microstate as the witness. ΦID atoms split that synergy into downward causation and causal decoupling, under stated axioms on the redundancy function, which the paper says the minimum-MI decomposition meets and which identity-respecting ones fail. The practical criteria Ψ, Δ, Γ are redundancy-free and sufficient only; as proved they certify the system's capacity, not the candidate feature. Applied to the Game of Life, boids and macaque ECoG. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-987](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-987.md)) in full; worth reading for the axioms the ΦID theory of causal emergence needs, the proof that a system hosts an emergent feature iff its parts carry synergy about their own future, the exact definitions of downward causation and causal decoupling, and the redundancy-free criteria Ψ, Δ, Γ. Read it knowing that the theorem's witness is the microstate itself; that Proposition 1, as proved, certifies the system's emergence capacity and not the candidate feature (under the minimum-MI decomposition the parity of two self-copying bits passes Ψ and is not emergent); that its axioms exclude identity-respecting redundancy measures and count aggregates of non-interacting persistent parts as emergent; and that Γ = 0 is never met in its data. |
| [LIT-1306](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1306.md) v2 | Software in the natural world: A computational approach to hierarchical emergence | Rosas, Geiger, Luppi, Seth, Polani, Gastpar & Mediano (arXiv 2024). Defines three exact closures of a coarse-graining Z of a stationary discrete process X. In informational closure the micro past adds nothing to predicting Z's future (Barnett–Seth dynamical independence). In causal closure Z's ε-machine equals its υ-machine, the coarsest partition of micro pasts that predicts Z. In computational closure Z's ε-machine is a coarse-graining of X's. It proves informational ⟺ causal closure, and causal ⇒ computational closure for spatial coarse-grainings, not conversely. It ties these to strong and weak lumpability of the micro ε-machine. It proposes the lattice of strongly lumpable coarse-grainings of that ε-machine, modulo computational equivalence, as a system's "functional architecture". The case studies are cellular-automaton parity, Ehrenfest, Glauber energy, a modular random walk, agent counts and Hopfield overlaps. Most of them close by a permutation symmetry. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1030](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1030.md)) in full; worth reading for three exact notions of a self-contained coarse-graining Z of a stationary discrete process X and how they relate: informational closure, I(X⃗_t; Z⃗ᴸ_{t+1} \| Z⃗_t) = 0 for every horizon, which is Barnett and Seth's dynamical independence without an environment; causal closure, the ε-machine of Z equivalent to its υ-machine (the coarsest partition of micro pasts that predicts Z's future); and computational closure, Z's ε-machine a coarse-graining of X's. Theorem 1 proves informational ⟺ causal closure for any coarse-graining of the past; Theorem 2 proves causal ⇒ computational closure for spatial ones, and Counterexample 4 the converse false. Proposition 4 and Theorem 3 tie closure to Kemeny–Snell lumpability: strong lumpability gives closure, closure with a Markov Z gives strong lumpability, weak lumpability gives only computational closure. Read it knowing that the sublattice claims are asserted and, for informationally closed spatial coarse-grainings, false under common refinement (a three-bit counterexample in the NOTE); that the stated sufficient condition for the Ising energy to close (a permutation-invariant Hamiltonian) fails with a uniform field at coincident energies; that Proposition 3 is a telescoping identity whose closure hypothesis is idle; that (A.11) and Example 2 contain slips; that the modular random walk closes by symmetry of the weights and not by modularity; and that every result is exact, with nothing on approximate closure. |
| [LIT-1310](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1310.md) v3 | Approximate Causal Abstractions | Beckers, Eberhardt & Halpern (2020; arXiv 2019). Extends exact causal abstraction to approximate abstraction: the worst case, over allowed interventions and contexts, of how far a high-level causal model's answers depart from the coarse-grained answers of the low-level model it abstracts, under a distance the user chooses; probabilistic versions average over contexts and, given an intervention distribution, over the low-level implementations of each high-level intervention. Composing an abstraction with an approximation gives an approximate abstraction, and the converse decomposition can fail. | Active — read 2026-10-21 ([NOTE-1045](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1045.md)) in full, from arXiv:1906.11583v2; worth reading for its distance between causal models that compares answers to interventions rather than graphs, for approximate abstraction as that distance under a coarse-graining ([THEORY-843](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-843.md)), for the intervention distribution over low-level implementations of a high-level intervention, and for when an approximate abstraction factors into an abstraction and an approximation. Read it knowing that the error is a worst case over interventions, minimized over context maps and relative to a metric the user chooses, so it is zero wherever exact abstraction holds, including coarse-grainings whose dropped detail high-level noise can carry. |
| [LIT-1316](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1316.md) v2 | Abstracting Causal Models | Beckers & Halpern (2019; arXiv 2018). A sequence of successively stronger definitions of abstraction between causal models, from Rubenstein et al.'s exact transformation through uniform transformation and abstraction to strong abstraction, which takes all potential interventions seriously, and constructive abstraction, which maps clusters of micro-variables to macro-variables; the paper says that combining micro-variables into macro-variables, and each of Rubenstein et al.'s examples, is constructive. | Active — read 2026-10-21 ([NOTE-1032](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1032.md)) in full, from arXiv:1812.03789v4; worth reading for the examples that show exact transformation too permissive, for the characterization of exactness under every distribution as a context map commuting with every allowed intervention ([THEORY-849](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-849.md)), and for the ladder τ-abstraction, strong and constructive abstraction. Read it knowing that its Theorem 3.8 omits the countability its proof uses, that the context map is only required to exist, so high-level noise may hold what the coarse state drops, and that every strong abstraction being constructive is a conjecture. |
| [LIT-1334](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1334.md) v2 | Causal Consistency of Structural Equation Models | Rubenstein, Weichwald, Bongers, Mooij, Janzing, Grosse-Wentrup & Schölkopf (2017). Defines an exact transformation between structural equation models, under which the models agree on the effects of a declared set of interventions, and shows that marginalising variables, aggregating micro-variables into macro-variables and moving from time series to equilibrium models can each be exact for the interventions declared. | Active — read 2026-10-21 ([NOTE-1037](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1037.md)) in full, from arXiv:1707.00819v1; worth reading for the definition of an exact transformation between structural equation models, with its order-preserving map on interventions, and for its three families of exact coarse-grainings: marginalisation ([THEORY-848](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-848.md)), averaging under equal column sums ([THEORY-847](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-847.md)) and equilibria. Read it knowing that exactness is equality of push-forward laws for a declared intervention set, which Beckers and Halpern show to be too permissive and which can drop a variable that decides how a system responds; that only perfect interventions are modelled; and that the coefficient of its Theorem 11, as extracted from this copy, appears to lack a factor n. |
| [LIT-1388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1388.md) v2 | The Political Legacy of American Slavery | Acharya, Blackwell and Sen (2016).
